title: Benchmarking large language model agent societies against human behavioural distributions
one_sentence: SILICA shows that rapid LLM naming-game convergence partly reflects shared label priors and apparatus sensitivity; negotiation becomes visible only after per-agent label-pool permutation.
problem: When may an LLM-agent social simulation support a human-behavior or convention claim rather than reproducing priors, presentation artifacts, or memorized experimental scripts?
method: Five human-anchored social environments, twelve open-weight models, 9,115 model runs, representation/design perturbations, divergent-payoff contamination tests, and a per-agent shuffled name-pool control.
findings: Seven of eight tested models still converged in every shuffled-pool seed, but 1.5–2.6 times more slowly; an eighth converged in only two of three seeds at 14–24 times the fixed-order time.
No assessed finding reached the paper's transferable tier; convention formation alone reached its robust tier, and no model matched the human tipping-point bracket.
real_contribution: Provides a concrete false-positive audit for computational convention claims and demonstrates why shared priors, label order, and apparatus perturbations must be separated from interaction-driven negotiation.
biggest_weakness: Single-author preprint; human evidence is imported as anchors, the key shuffled-pool control was added after transcript audit, and all agents still share pretrained label semantics.
claim_boundary: Supports an LLM-agent diagnostic precedent, not human-equivalent convention formation, human–AI grounding, embodiment, or mutual belief.
why_researcher_should_care: AMSC studies should counterbalance or individualize initial signal spaces and report robustness before attributing convergence to shared-history convention formation.

amsc.master_list_decision: Candidate — Must Read / Convention false-positive audit

evidence_notes: Open arXiv PDF inspected; v1 submitted 2026-08-28.
Agent-society results are not treated as evidence of human cognitive equivalence.
